short_summary: A former HR worker recounts his brief, grueling stint mulching parks for his brother's landscaping business during Covid-19 lockdowns, an experience that ultimately pushed him toward a career in journalism.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: A job that changed me: I mulched city parks in the dead of winter – I was not cut out for manual labour or working with family

paragraphs: In early 2020, as Covid lockdowns descended upon Canberra, Jack Larkin found himself at a personal crossroads. Having recently departed from a human resources position where the constant turnover of staff had left him disillusioned about long-term employment, Larkin retreated to his mother's house. Surrounded by empty beer cans, blaring sports broadcasts, and a glowing gaming setup, he faced two urgent pressures: he urgently required financial income, and his mother was eager to see him move out. The solution arrived in the form of his brother, who had recently established a landscaping enterprise and secured a municipal tender to spread mulch across city parks throughout Canberra.

Eager to secure employment, Larkin submitted a humorous landscaping CV that cited mowing his mother's lawn and trimming occasional hedges. To his surprise, he was hired, joining a colorful crew that included a former plasterer, an ex-sports physio, and a former rugby player. Every morning at five o'clock, the team crammed into a gritty Toyota HiLux, retrieved a skid steer loader, and headed to their designated park. The daily routine was monotonous: a truck would deliver a pile of mulch, the loader would transport portions to the base of trees, and the team would evenly distribute it using rakes before waiting idly for the next delivery.

Despite the repetitive nature of the tasks, unexpected moments of drama occasionally disrupted the monotony. Equipment failures, such as a loader breaking down in the middle of a road or a severely bent trailer jockey wheel, tested the crew's patience and physical strength. It soon became glaringly obvious to both Larkin and his brother that manual labor was not his forte. Months of sedentary indoor living had left his body unprepared for heavy physical exertion, frequently resulting in painful back spasms and dislocated shoulders. Furthermore, his tendency to lose focus and distract colleagues generated friction, leading to regular arguments with his brother regarding his work ethic.

Recognizing that their professional collaboration was straining their personal relationship, the brothers mutually agreed to terminate Larkin's short career in landscaping. Before parting ways on the project, his brother offered some candid advice, urging him to pursue higher education because he possessed a sharp mind rather than being suited for physical toil. Although initially surprised and slightly frustrated by the observation, Larkin eventually heeded similar advice that his parents had long given him. After a brief stint in communications, he relocated to Melbourne to study journalism, where he ultimately discovered his true professional calling.

Reflecting on that freezing winter, Larkin realized how profoundly that unconventional job shaped his perspective. While the extensive mulching project later proved counterproductive—reportedly triggering an outbreak of weeds that required subsequent de-mulching—and his brother's business eventually ceased operations a year later, the experience imparted a lasting lesson. It taught him the critical importance of engaging in mentally stimulating work that ignites genuine passion, proving that sometimes the wrong career path is precisely what is needed to illuminate the right one.

facts.fact: Jack Larkin left his HR job in early 2020 in Canberra during Covid lockdowns.
Needing money and pushed by his mother, Larkin joined his brother's landscaping business to mulch city parks.
The crew consisted of a ragtag team including an ex-sports physio, a former rugby player, and a former plasterer.
Larkin struggled with physical labor, suffered from back spasms, lacked focus, and frequently argued with his brother.
His brother ultimately advised him to quit and go to university, recognizing his intelligence.
Larkin later moved to Melbourne to study journalism and found his true calling.
